Social Justice
SOH-shul JUS-tis
noun phrase
The phrase enters wide use through the Jesuit Luigi Taparelli in the 1840s and the later social-encyclical tradition; in its origin it named the right ordering of society toward the common good. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries it was captured and redefined, especially through Rawlsian and critical-theory thought, into a program indexed to group identity and equality of outcome. The two senses now war under one label.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🟠
Examine
Biblical justice is impartial mishpat — render to each his due; the ideology re-indexes it to group identity. Distinguish the word, do not concede it.

📖 Biblical Definition

Scripture has a robust doctrine of justice, but it is mishpat — the impartial rendering to each man of what is due him. The law is exact: 'Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour' (Lev. 19:15). Justice is no respecter of persons; it neither flatters the great nor excuses the small. The LORD requires it of His people — 'to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God' (Mic. 6:8) — and joins it to righteousness, for 'justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne' (Ps. 89:14). This justice is fierce for the oppressed: 'learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow' (Isa. 1:17). But the standard is always God's law applied without partiality, rendering to each his due, never a re-distribution indexed to the group a man was born into.

📜 Origin & Era

Biblical justice is impartial mishpat — render to each his due, respect no persons (Lev. 19:15); the modern ideology bends 'justice' to group identity and equal outcomes. Distinguish the word, do not concede it.

SOCIAL JUSTICE, noun phrase. In origin, the right ordering of society toward the common good; in modern ideological use, a program of redistribution and standing indexed to group identity.

Biblical justice (Hebrew mishpat): impartial judgment rendering to each his due; 'thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty' (Lev. 19:15).

Modern capture: through Rawlsian and critical-theory thought, 'justice' is redefined as equity of outcome among identity groups rather than equity of judgment under one law.

The Christian distinguishes the two: he keeps the biblical kernel (judgment for the oppressed, Isa. 1:17) and rejects the ideological frame (partiality by group, condemned in Lev. 19:15 and Jas. 2:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:15 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."

Micah 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Isaiah 1:17 — "Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."

Psalm 89:14 — "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."

Deuteronomy 16:20 — "That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee."

Amos 5:24 — "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A good word with a real biblical kernel is captured by an ideology that re-indexes 'justice' from impartial judgment under God's law to equality of outcome among identity groups — the very respect of persons the law forbids.

expand to see more

The corruption is a substitution at the root of the word. Biblical justice answers the question 'what is due to this man under God's law?' and answers it without respect of persons, refusing alike to flatter the mighty and to excuse the poor (Lev. 19:15). The modern ideology answers a different question — 'how is power distributed among groups, and how shall it be re-distributed?' — and answers it precisely by respect of persons, treating a man's group identity as the decisive fact about his claims. The two are not the same justice with a social emphasis added; they rest on opposed principles. The first measures each case by an impartial law; the second measures cases by the group standing of the parties, which is the partiality the law condemns.

The trap is that the captured term keeps the moral weight of the true one. Because Scripture really does thunder for the oppressed — 'seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow' (Isa. 1:17) — the ideology drapes itself in those very texts, so that to question 'social justice' is made to sound like indifference to the poor. But the prophets never indexed justice to identity; they indexed it to righteousness. Amos cries 'let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream' (Amos 5:24) — judgment and righteousness together, one law for the small and the great (Deut. 1:17), not a sliding scale of claims by group. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: the modern 'social justice' frame and its identity/equity vocabulary are named here to rebut it.

The recovery is to refuse to surrender the word. The believer does not concede 'justice' to the ideology and retreat into private piety; he reclaims the term in its biblical fullness and distinguishes it sharply from the counterfeit. True justice is impartial, law-bound, and fiercely protective of the genuinely oppressed — the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, the wronged (Zech. 7:9-10) — rendering to each his due whatever his group. The church that learns to say 'this is justice, and that is not' has neither abandoned the oppressed nor swallowed the ideology; it has done the harder and better thing, which is to keep the word God gave it and mean by it what He means.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mishpat, impartial judgment rendering to each his due (Lev. 19:15); a good phrase captured to mean equality of outcome by group identity. Keep the biblical kernel; reject the ideological frame.

expand to see more

Hebrew: mishpat (H4941), judgment/justice — the impartial rendering to each of what is due (Lev. 19:15; Mic. 6:8).

History of the phrase: coined in the 1840s (Taparelli) for the common good, later captured by Rawlsian and critical-theory thought into identity-indexed equity.

The dividing line: Lev. 19:15 and Jas. 2:9 forbid respect of persons — impartial judgment, not group-indexed redistribution, is biblical justice.

Usage

"Scripture's justice is fierce for the widow and the fatherless, yet it respects no persons; the ideology's 'justice' does nothing but respect them, by group."

"He would not concede the word 'justice' to the activists; he reclaimed it — impartial, law-bound, and merciless toward partiality."

"Render to each his due under one law for small and great: that is mishpat, and a redistribution indexed to identity is not it."
